folder: C202 Ch 1: Strategic Human Resource Management

cards.front: Why does HRM count as a source of competitive advantage?
cards.answer: Every edge a firm has, from tech to cost to service, is built by people, and HRM shapes who they are and how they work.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.2
points: Competitive advantage = doing something differently from rivals that lets you outperform them
Talent matters most in knowledge-based firms, where people ARE the product
Examples: Patagonia, Apple, Zappos, Marriott

cards.front: What is human resource management (HRM)?
cards.answer: The function that attracts, hires, develops, rewards, and retains talent, and handles people issues and compliance.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.4
points: Also manages people-related risk and builds the overall talent system
Employee costs are one of the biggest budget items, so this is high stakes
History: first 'personnel' department at National Cash Register in 1901, after a strike

cards.front: How do 'should do', 'can do', and 'will do' differ in the HRM performance model?
cards.answer: Should = direction (planning, law); can = ability (staffing, training); will = motivation (pay, performance mgmt).
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.4
points: All three feed effective work processes, then competitive advantage, then org performance
Aligning all three maximizes motivation and advantage
Think: Does the employee know what to do? Are they able? Do they want to?

cards.front: Why are staffing and training called the foundation of the should/can/will model?
cards.answer: Incentives can't create ability; if people lack the talent or skills, no pay plan will fix their performance.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.4
points: Staffing brings in ability and motivation; training builds skills
Example: a nurse can't run a new machine just because you pay a bonus
Covered more in Ch 5-7

cards.front: How can a compensation system backfire on ethics?
cards.answer: Rewards tied to narrow targets can push people to cut corners to hit them, so HR must foresee unintended effects.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.4
points: Wells Fargo (2016): 5,000+ fired for opening fake accounts to hit sales quotas
Subprime mortgage brokers' bonuses rewarded risky loans
Lesson: design 'will do' systems by asking what behavior they might accidentally reward

cards.front: What is staffing, and what does it move through the organization?
cards.answer: Planning, acquiring, deploying, and retaining people; it moves talent into, through, and out of the firm.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.6
points: Steps: job requirements, sourcing, recruiting, retaining/moving, separations
Separations (layoffs, quits, terminations) are part of staffing
Its purpose is to help execute the business strategy
Caribou Coffee: careful hiring of store managers drove revenue

cards.front: Why is training wasted if performance management and rewards don't line up with it?
cards.answer: If reviews and pay don't recognize the new skills, people have little reason to use them on the job.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.7
points: HRM is a system of mutually reinforcing functions
Training is also wasted if hires can't succeed or quit before costs are recouped (some retail turnover ~200%)

cards.front: What is succession planning, and why does it matter?
cards.answer: Preparing people ahead of time to fill key roles, so leadership changes don't leave the company adrift.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.7
points: Citigroup started looking only after its CEO left and drifted
Google groomed Sundar Pichai for years: Google CEO 2015, Alphabet CEO 2019
CEO succession is often overlooked

cards.front: What is performance management?
cards.answer: Aligning employee goals and behavior with company strategy, appraising performance, and guiding improvement.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.8
points: Depends on staffing (raw talent) and development (fixing gaps)
Often tied to pay, so biased ratings demotivate people

cards.front: Why do specific goals and frequent feedback improve performance?
cards.answer: Goals show people what to aim for; feedback shows how they're doing so they can adjust before it's too late.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.8
points: No goals: unclear focus, underperformance, quits (which burdens staffing)
Feedback that feels unfair lowers effort
Performance feedback also maintains ethical behavior and communicates expectations

cards.front: What does 'total rewards' include?
cards.answer: Everything an employee gets for their time and effort: direct pay, benefits, and nonfinancial rewards.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.9
points: Judge job offers on total rewards, not salary alone
In the textbook's pie chart, nonfinancial rewards are roughly half

cards.front: How do direct and indirect financial compensation differ?
cards.answer: Direct is cash-type pay like salary, bonuses, and stock options; indirect is benefits like insurance and PTO.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.9
points: Direct: salary, wages, commissions, bonuses, stock options
Indirect (benefits): health insurance, wellness, paid vacation, free meals, retirement

cards.front: What is nonfinancial compensation?
cards.answer: Intrinsic rewards from the work or its setting, such as feeling successful, valued, or appreciated.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.9
points: Not money and not a benefit, but still a real part of total rewards
Examples: meaningful work, recognition, a supportive team

cards.front: How do pay level and staffing influence each other?
cards.answer: Premium pay lets you recruit top candidates; low pay may force you to hire less-ready people and train more.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.9
points: Incentive pay also depends on accurate performance management
Top pay isn't always needed: does every marketer need an MBA?

cards.front: Why can paying well above market still be cost-effective?
cards.answer: Higher pay can cut turnover and raise productivity, so labor cost per sale stays competitive and service improves.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.9
points: Costco pays well above Sam's Club yet gets similar labor returns
Lower turnover also means lower hiring and training costs

cards.front: Why does health and safety pay off for the business, not just ethically?
cards.answer: Healthier, safer workers are more productive and cut insurance, workers' comp costs, and lost time.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.10
points: Safety = protection from toxins, accidents, injuries; health = physical AND mental
About half of U.S. worksites offer wellness programs
Provide gear, train on it, hold people accountable; many federal/state laws apply (Ch 12)

cards.front: What does employee-management relations cover?
cards.answer: The relationship and rights between employees and employer, including union bargaining and employee voice.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.11
points: Tools: participation programs, employee surveys
In union settings, employers must bargain in good faith; contracts set terms
2019 union membership: 33.6% public sector vs 6.2% private

cards.front: What does it mean for HR functions to be 'aligned'?
cards.answer: They all reinforce the same behaviors and never undercut each other, so they work as one integrated system.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.11
points: Example of misalignment: training teamwork but paying only for individual results
SAS: trust-based culture, results-based reviews, and rich benefits all point the same way

cards.front: What are the two broad ways HRM adds value to an organization?
cards.answer: By improving efficiency (getting more from resources) and by contributing to revenue growth.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.12
points: Other effects: clearer responsibilities, better skills use, higher engagement, better change mgmt, less turnover
Also lowers legal liability
Good people practices linked to up to 30% higher firm value (Watson Wyatt)

cards.front: How do strategic and operational HR risk differ?
cards.answer: Strategic risk covers talent strategy, culture, and ethics; operational risk is how well you hire, grow, keep people.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.12
points: Strategic: talent strategy, culture, ethics, people investment, change
Operational: speed and effectiveness of hiring, developing, retaining top performers

cards.front: How do financial and compliance HR risk differ?
cards.answer: Financial risk is about people costs like pay and turnover; compliance risk is legal, like safety and harassment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.12
points: Financial: pay, benefits, turnover, overtime, time-to-hire, errors, accidents
Compliance: diversity, safety, unions, whistleblowers, harassment
Moody's bond ratings even factor in recruiting, retention, and training

cards.front: What is a business strategy?
cards.answer: How a company chooses to compete, based on what customers want and what it can deliver cost-effectively.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.13
points: Can differ across business units
HRM must fit the strategy, and the strategy must fit the competitive environment

cards.front: What is a talent philosophy?
cards.answer: A company's beliefs about how employees should be treated, e.g., as long-term partners or replaceable inputs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.13
points: Covers diversity, ethics, short vs career-long tenure, assets vs investors of their time
Usually shaped by founders
Goldman Sachs: people are our greatest asset; diverse staff serves diverse clients

cards.front: How do HR strategy and strategic HRM differ?
cards.answer: HR strategy ties HR to business strategy; strategic HRM aligns employee and company goals within each HR function.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.13
points: Strategic HRM shapes the strategy of each HR function
Aligned functions form an integrated HRM system guided by the talent philosophy

cards.front: What is a global mindset, and how do you get one?
cards.answer: The ability to influence people from very different cultures and systems; it's built through experience.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.14
points: i4cp: cross-cultural influence matters more than basic business skills ('table stakes')
HSBC sends new managers on long international assignments to build it

cards.front: How should power distance shape HR practices in another country?
cards.answer: In high power-distance cultures, empowering employees can clash with norms, so practices should fit local culture.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.14
points: Small power distance: U.S., Sweden, Germany; large: Japan, Mexico
Cultures also differ in motivation, communication style, family vs work emphasis

cards.front: How do operational excellence and product innovation strategies need different HRM?
cards.answer: Operational excellence stresses cost control and consistency; innovation needs creative hires and room to experiment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.15
points: Operational excellence: lean pay/benefits, teamwork, standard procedures
Innovation (Apple, 3M, pharma): hire for creativity, analysis, teamwork; reward persistence
Porter: advantage = better product at a premium or good product for less

cards.front: What HR approach fits a customer intimacy (customization) strategy?
cards.answer: Hiring and developing people who learn customers' needs and can flex service, often with heavy HR investment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.15
points: Common in consulting, retail, banking
Starbucks: hires active learners with customer skills and emotional resilience

cards.front: Why do mergers and acquisitions so often fail?
cards.answer: The combining firms' cultures, values, or structures clash, more often than any technical or financial issue.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.15
points: M&A is a common route to growth and international expansion
Failures: DaimlerChrysler, HP-Compaq, AOL-Time Warner
Check culture fit before the deal

cards.front: Why is every supervising manager responsible for HRM?
cards.answer: HR supplies the tools, but managers use them daily; the system only works if managers apply them well.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.16
points: HR is a support function: interview guides, review forms, etc.
Mattel made managers true partners in managing talent
Employees also own pieces: their own development, records, certifications

cards.front: How does a PEO differ from a shared service center?
cards.answer: A PEO is an outside firm that becomes the legal employer; a shared service center is an in-house hub for routine HR.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.16
points: PEO: leases workers for ~2-7% of gross wages; handles payroll, benefits, training, discipline
Shared service center: centralizes payroll/benefits transactions (Home Depot HR call centers)
Outsourcing to vendors is a third option, especially for small firms

cards.front: Why did IBM separate core HR roles from administrative ones?
cards.answer: Centralizing routine admin freed HR experts to focus on strategic work like talent, leadership, and upskilling.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.17
points: Admin (payroll, expenses, records) moved to global service centers
Also replaced annual reviews with frequent feedback via the employee-designed Checkpoint app
Goal: right talent, right time, right place

cards.front: What is an HRMS, and how should a firm choose one?
cards.answer: A tech platform for employee records, recruiting, and analytics; choose based on real intended use and ease of use.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.19
points: Cloud (Workday, Cornerstone OnDemand) or in-house
Increasingly integrates apps and supports continuous feedback

cards.front: How does Patagonia's HR reinforce its business strategy?
cards.answer: It hires for mission fit and offers cause-driven benefits, building a loyal workforce with very low turnover.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.20
points: Paid environmental volunteering, bail for peaceful protest, on-site childcare
Nearly 100% of new mothers return; ~4% turnover; ~9,000 applicants for few openings
Strategy: high-quality, responsibly made gear; 'do well and do good'

cards.front: What does SHRM's code ask of HR professionals?
cards.answer: Act ethically, obey the law, measure HR's impact, and openly advocate for fair treatment of people.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.18
points: SHRM = largest HR professional association
Professional responsibility: add value, own your decisions, advocate for the profession

cards.front: Exit interviews show new hires at a call center quit because nobody told them the job requires rotating weekend shifts. HR rewrites job postings and adds a realistic job preview. Which HR function is this?
cards.explanation: Defining job requirements and recruiting people who will accept and stay in the role is staffing. Fixing the front end of hiring prevents the turnover.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.6 Apply

cards.front: A firm's new strategy needs reps to cross-sell. The reps know how and would earn commission for it, but no one told them it's a priority and their job descriptions still say 'take orders.' Which element is missing?
cards.explanation: They have the ability (can do) and the incentive (will do), but no direction. Planning and job design tell people what they should do.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.4 Apply

cards.front: A startup's sales reps don't understand the product. The CEO's fix is a huge commission bonus. What's the flaw?
choices: Pay can't supply missing ability; this is a staffing or training gap
Bonuses are a form of indirect compensation
The reps should be moved to a PEO
Nothing; motivation is always the issue
cards.explanation: Incentives affect 'will do,' not 'can do.' If people lack knowledge, you need better hiring or training first.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.4 Apply

cards.front: A company pays bonuses only on the number of new accounts opened. Months later an audit finds many accounts were never authorized by customers. What went wrong?
choices: The reward created an incentive to game the metric
cards.explanation: A narrow target rewarded volume regardless of how it was reached. Wells Fargo is the real example. Good 'will do' design anticipates unintended consequences.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.4 Apply

cards.front: A hospital trains nurses on a new safety checklist, but annual reviews and raises are based only on patients seen per shift. Nurses skip the checklist. Best diagnosis?
choices: HR functions are misaligned and work against each other
cards.explanation: Training teaches one behavior while performance management and pay reward another. Functions must reinforce the same behaviors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.11 Apply

cards.front: Offer A: $80K, few benefits. Offer B: $74K plus full health coverage, a 6% retirement match, tuition aid, and flexible hours. How should you compare them?
choices: Pick A; salary is what counts
Compare total rewards across both offers
Pick whichever has the bigger bonus
Ignore benefits since they aren't compensation
cards.explanation: Total rewards includes direct pay, benefits (indirect), and nonfinancial rewards. B's benefits may be worth far more than $6K.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.9 Apply

cards.front: Which of these is indirect financial compensation?
choices: Public recognition at a team meeting
cards.explanation: Indirect financial compensation is benefits like wellness, insurance, and PTO. Bonuses and options are direct; recognition is nonfinancial.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.9 Apply

cards.front: An employee files a harassment complaint, and HR learns that supervisors were never trained on the anti-harassment policy. Which HR risk is most exposed?
cards.explanation: Harassment, safety, unions, and whistleblowers fall under compliance risk because they involve legal obligations.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.12 Apply

cards.front: Overtime spending has doubled and payroll errors are causing costly corrections. Which HR risk category is this?
cards.explanation: Pay, overtime, turnover costs, and costly errors are financial risk: the direct money impact of people practices.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.12 Apply

cards.front: A budget airline competes on the lowest fares. Which HR approach fits its strategy best?
choices: Premium pay to lure star talent
Tight cost control, standard procedures, and teamwork
Hire creative risk-takers and fund experiments
Deep client knowledge and custom service
cards.explanation: Low fares mean an operational excellence strategy: lean costs, consistent procedures, and teamwork on thin margins.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.15 Apply

cards.front: A biotech wants to beat rivals with breakthrough therapies. Which hiring focus fits?
choices: Analytical and creative people who persist through failure
cards.explanation: A product innovation strategy needs an innovative culture and people with analytical and creative ability who keep going through setbacks.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.15 Apply

cards.front: A boutique wealth-management firm wins clients by tailoring advice to each family's situation. Which competitive strategy is this?
cards.explanation: Customization depends on knowing customers deeply and flexing service, so HR invests in hiring and developing people with strong client skills.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.15 Apply

cards.front: A manager ignores the structured interview guide HR provided and hires on gut feel. The hire flops. Who is most directly responsible?
choices: The manager, because managers carry out HRM day to day
The HR department, since it owns hiring
cards.explanation: HR supplies tools, but they only add value if supervising managers use them. Every manager owns part of HRM.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.16 Apply

cards.front: A 40-person landscaping company has no HR staff. It wants payroll, benefits, and workers' comp handled, plus the flexibility to shrink its workforce in winter. Best option?
cards.explanation: A PEO becomes the legal employer, handles payroll, benefits, and admin, and lets the client simply not renew leased workers in a downturn.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.16 Apply

cards.front: A 30,000-employee retailer has every store handling its own payroll and benefits questions, with inconsistent results. They want to keep the work in-house. Best fix?
cards.explanation: Shared service centers centralize routine HR transactions in-house, cutting redundancy and cost while improving consistency.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.16 Apply

cards.front: A VP pressures an HR manager to quietly bury an employee's safety complaint. What do SHRM's ethical standards point toward?
choices: Comply, since the VP outranks HR
Refuse and raise it through proper channels, protecting legal compliance and fair treatment
Leak it to the media right away
Drop it, since safety isn't an HR issue
cards.explanation: SHRM's code calls for obeying the law, high ethical standards, and openly advocating for proper treatment of people through appropriate forums.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.18 Apply

cards.front: A U.S. firm opens an office in a high power-distance country and launches a 'challenge your boss' empowerment program. Few employees take part. Likely reason?
choices: The program clashes with local norms about hierarchy
cards.explanation: In high power-distance cultures, people expect clear hierarchy, so empowerment programs can feel inappropriate. Fit HR practices to the local culture.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.14 Apply

cards.front: A company is choosing an HRMS. Which factor should matter most?
choices: How the firm will actually use it and how easy it is for managers and employees
cards.explanation: Pick an HRMS for its real intended use and ease of use. Unused features add cost without adding value.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.19 Apply

cards.front: A CEO worries that fast growth has weakened the company's ethics and culture. Which category of HR risk is this?
cards.explanation: Talent strategy, culture, ethics awareness, and change all fall under strategic risk.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.12 Practice

cards.front: For HR functions to support rather than undermine each other, they need to be consistent in...
choices: How long they've been in place
cards.explanation: Alignment means every function, from hiring and training to pay and reviews, pushes toward the same behaviors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.11 Practice

cards.front: Small businesses most often report which two areas as their biggest management problems?
cards.explanation: Recruitment and training are top problems, especially for small firms with no HR budget. That's why HR is an investment, not just a cost.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.7 Practice

cards.front: A company is restructuring and downsizing. Which group is usually expected to lead the organizational change?
cards.explanation: HR professionals lead organizational change like expansion, restructuring, and downsizing, using communication, influence, and leadership skills.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.16 Practice

cards.front: When you boil it down, what is HRM ultimately trying to do for a company?
choices: Be the main contact for shareholders
Reduce people-related risk and keep strong performers
cards.explanation: HRM manages people risk (legal, financial, strategic) and builds a talent system that keeps great employees. The other options belong to other functions.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q1

cards.front: A CFO asks how HR actually creates value. What's the best answer?
choices: Hiring only people with advanced degrees
Helping the company carry out its business strategy
Keeping pay as low as possible
cards.explanation: HRM creates value by helping execute business strategy, getting the right people with the right skills and motivation in place.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q2

cards.front: Which sequence best captures HRM's core purpose across the employee life cycle?
cards.explanation: HRM attracts, hires, develops, rewards, and retains talent. Each verb maps to an HR function.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q3

cards.front: A plant switches to a new assembly process, and workers need new skills to run it. Which HR function steps in?
cards.explanation: Building current employees' skills for new methods is training and development. Staffing would bring in new people instead.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q4

cards.front: Staffing isn't just filling seats. It exists to help the company carry out its ___ strategy.
cards.explanation: Staffing plans, acquires, deploys, and retains talent so the firm can execute its business strategy.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q5

cards.front: Layoffs, resignations, and firings for poor performance fall under which HR function?
cards.explanation: Staffing moves talent into, through, AND out of the organization, so separations are part of it.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q6

cards.front: A company grooms several high-potential managers years in advance so it's ready if the COO leaves. What is this called?
cards.explanation: Succession planning prepares people to fill key positions and reduces disruption during transitions (think Google and Pichai).
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q7

cards.front: Which HR function makes sure what individual employees aim for lines up with what the organization is trying to achieve?
cards.explanation: Performance management aligns employee goals and behavior with organizational goals, then appraises and improves performance.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q8

cards.front: If staffing brings in the wrong people, which two other functions feel the impact most directly?
cards.explanation: Staffing supplies the raw talent. Development has to fill the gaps, and performance management depends on that talent being there.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q9

cards.front: A manager wants to reinforce ethical conduct day to day. According to the chapter, which kind of feedback serves that purpose?
cards.explanation: Performance feedback, part of performance management, tells people how they're doing, communicates expectations, and helps maintain ethical behavior.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q10

cards.front: A job offer lists base salary, a signing bonus, sales commission, and stock options. Together these are...
cards.explanation: Salary, wages, commissions, bonuses, and stock options are direct financial compensation, paid directly for work.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q11

cards.front: Employer-paid health insurance, paid vacation, and a retirement plan are examples of...
cards.explanation: Benefits are indirect financial compensation: they have money value but aren't paid as cash for performance.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q12

cards.front: An analyst says the best part of her job is the sense of accomplishment and feeling appreciated by her team. Which reward category is that?
cards.explanation: Intrinsic rewards from the work or environment, like feeling successful or valued, are nonfinancial compensation.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q13

cards.front: One major way effective HRM boosts organizational performance is by building...
cards.explanation: HRM adds value by improving efficiency (efficient systems and processes) and by contributing to revenue growth.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q14

cards.front: Three of these are outcomes of an effective HRM system. Which one is NOT?
choices: Tying rewards fairly to responsibility and performance
Reporting ethics violations to the Bureau of Labor Statistics
cards.explanation: The BLS is a statistics agency; reporting ethics breaches to it isn't an HRM outcome. The others are listed benefits of effective HRM.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q15

cards.front: The strategy that defines where and how a company competes in its market is its ___ strategy.
cards.explanation: Business strategy is how a firm competes and positions itself. HR strategy must then fit it.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q16

cards.front: A founder believes employees are long-term partners worth investing in, not interchangeable parts. This set of beliefs about how people should be treated is the company's...
cards.explanation: A talent philosophy is the firm's beliefs about how employees should be treated. It guides the integrated HRM system. ('Employee philosophy' is the tempting wrong pick.)
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q17

cards.front: Which approach do firms commonly use to expand quickly into new countries?
cards.explanation: Mergers and acquisitions are a common route to growth and international expansion, and a way to acquire talent.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q18

cards.front: Two companies merge. The deal looks great on paper but falls apart within two years. What's the most common culprit?
cards.explanation: M&A deals most often fail because cultures, values, or structures clash (DaimlerChrysler, AOL-Time Warner).
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q19

cards.front: Which document is the go-to reference that helps employees understand company HR policies?
cards.explanation: Employee handbooks, often online, document HR policies and serve as a reference for employees.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q20
